new_statements.quote: 3.1. Inventory. There are five tones in Banda-Tangbago: High (´), Mid (¯), Low (`), Falling (^), and Rising (ˇ). An allotone of Low occurring utterance final glides from low pitch to extra low pitch. [...] 3.3. Functional load. Tone has lexical function in all word classes. In verbs and pronouns, it has grammatical function as well [...] 4.1. Configurations. There are two syllable configurations in Banda-Tangbago, V and CV. [...] Every syllable carries a tone. 4.2. Strong and weak. For the sake of convenience, CV syllables composed of a liquid and a low vowel are termed strong. Preceding CV syllables composed of a non-liquid and a simple vowel are termed weak.
new_statements.citation: Sampson, Douglas L. 1985. The phonology of Banda-Tangbago. In Russell G. Schuh (ed.), Papers from the fifteenth conference on African linguistics (Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 9), 269-274. Los Angeles: UCLA.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.1 'Tone: Inventory', sec. 3.3 'Functional load', sec. 4.1-4.2 'Syllables', p. 271 (pdf p. 279 of the full issue; p. 3 of the split file)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda-Tangbago is described as a five-tone language (three level tones plus falling and rising) in which every syllable bears a tone and tone is lexically contrastive in all word classes and grammatically contrastive in verbs and pronouns. The description contains no statement about word stress or accent at all; its 'strong' vs 'weak' syllables are a segmental classification (liquid + low vowel vs other CV) used to state vowel-distribution restrictions, not a stress position. No word-stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: nouns usually carry only level tones (all 9 two-syllable and 27 three-syllable level-tone combinations attested); verbs lack Rising; adjectives carry level, usually identical, tones (sec. 3.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of the Tangbago dialect recorded at Sopo, Sudan, 1982-83 (sec. 0). Sec. 8 'Intonation' describes only paragraph-level pitch register (higher onset, lower final phrase; a high register for questions/astonishment), explicitly not much contrastive intonation. Tone-mark glyphs in the quote are normalized from a garbled scanned layer; the wording is verbatim.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened primary description (Sampson 1985) covers the Tangbago dialect, studied at Sopo, South Sudan, in 1982-83. Glottolog's own coding of that reference is 'Tangbago = Banda-Ndélé [bfl]' (ref 99632) and Moñino 1988 (via Wikipedia 'Central Banda language') lists Tàngbàgò among the Bàndà-Ndele varieties, so the identity with band1345 is secure; Glottolog lists no separate dialect glottocode for Tangbago. Note that Glottolog's Cloarec-Heiss 1986 grammar attached to this languoid is coded for Banda-Bambari [liy] (Banda-Linda), not bfl.

sources.note: Nothing: the words stress/accent/prominence never occur (grep 0 hits). Sec. 3 describes five tones (H, M, L, Falling, Rising), every syllable carries a tone, tone is lexical in all word classes and grammatical in verbs/pronouns; sec. 4.2 'strong'/'weak' syllables are defined segmentally (liquid + low vowel = strong), not as stress; sec. 8 intonation is paragraph-level register only.
